newsitem.title: GERMANY: German flood-hit villagers welcome Bonn aid.
newsitem.headline: German flood-hit villagers welcome Bonn aid.

text.p: Villagers on Tuesday welcomed Bonn's efforts to keep potentially catastrophic floods at bay and rebuild the devastated region, as water levels fell back and the worst appeared to be over.
Politicians called the huge relief operation a token of solidarity between Germany's former Communist east and affluent west. Villagers said the crisis had brought them closer.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl pledged up to 500 million marks ($268.3 million) in federal government aid to the region along the Oder River, calling floods there in the past weeks the "worst natural disaster ever faced by newly-unified Germany".
Soldiers started to clean up villages that had been sandbagged to the hilt to hold back the surging Oder that forms part of Germany's border with Poland.
The work was in full swing in Ratzdorf, 50 km south of Frankfurt an der Oder at the confluence of the Oder and Neisse rivers, where officials said water levels were falling rapidly.

"We are very grateful for the help Bonn is providing," Ratzdorf's mayor, Ute Petzel, said, referring to plans to create 10,000 jobs to reconstruct the area in the wake of the worst floods in living memory.
"We have about 20 percent unemployed in Ratzdorf. People here don't want charity. This is exactly what they want -- to be given the chance to rebuild the area themselves".
Announcing the new aid package, Kohl did not specify whether it would take the form of direct government grants or available as soft loans, such as a 200-million-mark credit already announced.

Ironically, his announcement came as Bonn sources said the government planned a two-percentage-point cut in the "solidarity tax", an unpopular levy on incomes intended to finance economic regeneration in the region.
But inhabitants of the flood region were in no mood to be critical, praising government efforts that came as something as a surprise to them.
"We never expected such support and we have been really impressed by the enormous efforts of the German army to secure our homes," said Ratzdorf resident Eveline Krueger, 55.
She praised Defence Minister Volker Ruehe who promised to keep 10,000 troops, who had been securing flood barriers along the river, to stay on and help clean up villages.
"Because of this support, we have been able to feel safe at night in our beds," said Krueger, standing outside her house which was narrowly saved from flooding by the wall of army sandbags.
"It's brought people in the village closer together. Before it was every man for himself," said resident Christiane Sass.
Manfred Stolpe, premier of the flood-hit state of Brandenburg, hailed the efforts of thousands of soldiers and aid workers at a special session of the Bundestag lower house of parliament in Bonn.

"In the seventh year after unification the German nation has passed its probation test on the Oder dikes," said Stolpe, who was once a native of the former communist country and is today one of east Germany's most popular politicians.
The Oder was swollen by the same rains that caused flooding in the Czech Republic and Poland last month claiming more than 100 lives and causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.
Germany has escaped the worst of the floods, but damage to homes, businesses and farms has been extensive.

For the first time in the two-week flood crisis in eastern Germany, soldiers who had battled round the clock to reinforce dikes protecting the low-lying Oderbruch region stopped sandbagging and even started removing the bags from some areas.
No new tears appeared in dikes overnight and water levels, which started dropping on Sunday for the first time in three weeks, had fallen by up to a metre in some areas.
President Roman Herzog, visiting the flood-stricken area, said mass flooding had been avoided on the fertile Oderbruch plain because of the "fantastic" effort by soldiers.
Kohl, announcing the aid package in parliament, said the whole country was proud of the operation, which showed that the Bundeswehr was the "army of our people".

But local officials said emergency measures would remain in place for the time being. They said river levels, edging down by centimetres each day, still had to drop 1.5 metres before the worst was over, adding it could take until Friday.

A Berlin-based government health agency said inhabitants in the region would be at risk from typhoid, hepatatis A and bacterial diarrhoea for weeks, especially as more people came into contact with infected water in the clean-up operation.
